explanation: The original project asks when actual OO architecture boundaries win, fail or reverse under later requirements. This tests time-indexed route-boundary installation vs later repair, not a new universal SOLID law.

costs_separate.S: actual number of route registrations in source architecture at each phase (not function points)
costs_separate.L: number of additional authored source registration operations to handle late demand (not engineering hours or actual upstream patch lines)
costs_separate.C: named old/new client capability requirements and conformance only; no full bundled interface burden inferred
costs_separate.A: local user-authorized research fixture only, historical upstream merge permission UNKNOWN
costs_separate.Q: native pinned original Echo router actual HTTP behavior

before_execution_hypotheses: Both SINGLE and SPLIT have exactly equal declared initial client results.
SINGLE uses one router registration in initial source; SPLIT uses two.
For late legacy clients, SINGLE fails until adding a sibling generic handler; SPLIT works without later source edit.
After late repair, SINGLE_REPAIRED and SPLIT satisfy same declared clients. Under no late demand, SINGLE retains strictly smaller initial registration surface.
Total source route registrations under late demand become equal; no overall lifecycle scalar-winner or strict full-life sign reversal is presumed.
Registration order of generic and literal-inline route is a separate possible source moderator; verify in original source rather than assuming commutation.
rival_type: source-realized AUTHOR-DEFINED ARCHITECTURE ASSEMBLIES using unchanged original upstream router; NOT original maintainer alternatives
classically_explainable: basic real-options tradeoff, source-edit timing, frame and contextual refinement; no prior-art superiority claimed
prohibits: claim net life-cycle superiority from one extra route
